    Solution

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Uses 1+r1+r1+r in the denominator instead of 1−r1-r1−r.

    You chose C: Divides the first term by the second instead of the second by the first, inverting the ratio.

    You chose D: Multiplies aaa by 1−r1-r1−r instead of dividing by it.

    S=121−(−13)=1243=9.S = \frac{12}{1-\left(-\tfrac13\right)} = \frac{12}{\tfrac43} = 9.S=1−(−31​)12​=34​12​=9.

  14. 14

    What happens to the partial sums of the series 11−11+11−11+⋯11 - 11 + 11 - 11 + \cdots11−11+11−11+⋯?

    Answer choices for question 14

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Assumes every divergent series must grow past every bound, missing the case where partial sums stay bounded but never settle.

    You chose B: Treats the series as if it telescopes to a single value by naive cancellation, ignoring that a sum is defined by where the PARTIAL sums settle, not by pairing terms.

    You chose D: Applies the sum formula outside its required condition ∣r∣<1|r|<1∣r∣<1; at r=−1r=-1r=−1 the formula is not entitled to mean anything.

    List a few partial sums directly.

    S1=11,S2=0,S3=11,S4=0,…S_1=11,\quad S_2=0,\quad S_3=11,\quad S_4=0,\ldotsS1​=11,S2​=0,S3​=11,S4​=0,…

    The values never grow, but they never settle on one number either, so the series diverges without running away.

    The answer

    Part A

    (n2)=n(n−1)2\binom{n}{2}=\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}(2n​)=2n(n−1)​; (n3)=n(n−1)(n−2)6\binom{n}{3}=\tfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}(3n​)=6n(n−1)(n−2)​.

    Part B

    n=14n=14n=14; check: (143)=364=4(142)=4(91)\binom{14}{3}=364=4\binom{14}{2}=4(91)(314​)=364=4(214​)=4(91).

    Part C

    The other two roots are n=0n=0n=0 and n=1n=1n=1, and neither is valid: (n3)\binom{n}{3}(3n​) requires choosing 333 items from a set of nnn, which only makes sense when n≥3n\ge3n≥3, so those roots satisfy the cleared algebraic equation without corresponding to a genuine value of the original binomial coefficients.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Cancel the shared factorial tail in each closed form.

    (n2)=n!2!(n−2)!=n(n−1)(n−2)!2(n−2)!=n(n−1)2,(n3)=n!3!(n−3)!=n(n−1)(n−2)6.\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n!}{2!(n-2)!}=\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)!}{2(n-2)!}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}, \qquad \binom{n}{3}=\frac{n!}{3!(n-3)!}=\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}.(2n​)=2!(n−2)!n!​=2(n−2)!n(n−1)(n−2)!​=2n(n−1)​,(3n​)=3!(n−3)!n!​=6n(n−1)(n−2)​.

    Part B

    Substitute the expressions from part A.

    n(n−1)(n−2)6=4⋅n(n−1)2=2n(n−1).\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6} = 4\cdot\frac{n(n-1)}{2} = 2n(n-1).6n(n−1)(n−2)​=4⋅2n(n−1)​=2n(n−1).

    Since n≥3n\ge3n≥3 makes n(n−1)≠0n(n-1)\ne0n(n−1)=0, divide both sides by it.

    n−26=2⟹n−2=12⟹n=14.\frac{n-2}{6}=2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n-2=12 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=14.6n−2​=2⟹n−2=12⟹n=14.

    Check: (142)=91\binom{14}{2}=91(214​)=91 and (143)=364=4(91)\binom{14}{3}=364=4(91)(314​)=364=4(91).

    Part C

    Setting each factor of n(n−1)(n−14)=0n(n-1)(n-14)=0n(n−1)(n−14)=0 to zero gives three candidate roots.

    n=0,n=1,n=14.n=0, \qquad n=1, \qquad n=14.n=0,n=1,n=14.

    But n=0n=0n=0 and n=1n=1n=1 are not valid for the ORIGINAL equation. The closed forms from part A, (n2)=n(n−1)2\binom{n}{2}=\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}(2n​)=2n(n−1)​ and (n3)=n(n−1)(n−2)6\binom{n}{3}=\tfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}(3n​)=6n(n−1)(n−2)​, are algebraic expressions that can be evaluated at any nnn, but (nk)\binom{n}{k}(kn​) itself, as a count of ways to choose kkk items from nnn, is only defined when 0≤k≤n0\le k\le n0≤k≤n. Choosing 333 items requires a set of at least 333 to choose from, so (n3)\binom{n}{3}(3n​) has no meaning at all when n=0n=0n=0 or n=1n=1n=1, even though its closed-form expression can still be evaluated there.

    Clearing fractions turned the original relationship between two binomial coefficients into a purely algebraic polynomial equation, and that wider equation picked up two extra roots that the closed-form expressions satisfy but that the original counting problem never could. That is exactly why the problem restricts attention to n≥3n\ge3n≥3 in the first place: it is the domain where (n2)\binom{n}{2}(2n​) and (n3)\binom{n}{3}(3n​) are both genuinely defined, and n=14n=14n=14 is the only root of the cleared equation that lands inside it.

    In one line

    (n2)=n(n−1)2\binom{n}{2}=\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}(2n​)=2n(n−1)​ and (n3)=n(n−1)(n−2)6\binom{n}{3}=\tfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}(3n​)=6n(n−1)(n−2)​; solving (n3)=4(n2)\binom{n}{3}=4\binom{n}{2}(3n​)=4(2n​) gives n=14n=14n=14 (checked: 364=4(91)364=4(91)364=4(91)). The cleared equation n(n−1)(n−14)=0n(n-1)(n-14)=0n(n−1)(n−14)=0 also has roots n=0n=0n=0 and n=1n=1n=1, but (n3)\binom{n}{3}(3n​) is only defined when n≥3n\ge3n≥3, so those roots satisfy the algebraic equation without describing a genuine row and are excluded by the problem's restriction.
